posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging on a compliance-driven AI trust post — validate the explainability problem as the core issue, not AI itself, and add the insight that auditability is what separates useful AI from liability
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is exactly where things fall apart in regulated environments. It's not really an AI problem — it's an auditability problem. The question isn't whether AI touched the number, it's whether you can trace it back through every step if someone asks. I wonder how many teams are quietly running into this before a regulator is the one who surfaces it.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that dashboards don't fail on data quality, they fail on accountability for the numbers
posts.draft_comment: 18 months is about right for the build. The trust part though — that's a different problem entirely, and it's not really about the tool. It's about who owns the numbers. If nobody's accountable for the figure in the dashboard being *the* figure, people will always find a reason to run their own version in Excel. Whose job is it at Greenfield to say 'this number is right, full stop'?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a way of saying 'we don't know what matters yet' — and most teams never admit that out loud. The jump to 85% usage tells the real story though. It's not that people didn't want the data, they just couldn't see themselves in it. What was the hardest metric to cut?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at a retail brand is engaging on a post about data chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a governance problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing is so consistent it's almost a law of BI. You give people the ability to build their own reports and what you've actually done is decentralised the argument about what numbers mean — not solved it. The tool was never really the problem. Has anyone actually cracked this without just appointing someone whose full-time job is being right?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the framing, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think most analytics vendors have caught up to it yet. A hallucinated number that reaches a decision-maker isn't a UX problem — it's a trust failure with real downstream consequences. The part that keeps me up at night is that most teams have no audit trail to even know it happened. Who in your org is actually responsible when a bad AI output drives a bad call?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post that nails Milo's core pain point — validate the systemic failure, add the real reason it happens, no pitch needed
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number is almost a distraction — we've seen the same thing happen with £20k tools. The real problem is that most BI platforms are designed to be configured by someone technical and then handed over, which just doesn't work. Business teams don't need training, they need a tool that thinks the way they do. How many times does this have to happen before buyers start asking vendors to prove it in week one, not year one?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' crisis — validate the culture diagnosis but add the missing layer about why culture alone isn't enough without a single source of truth
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one very uncomfortable CFO — that's not a data problem, that's a trust problem. And you're right that AI doesn't fix it. But I'd push back slightly on 'culture will' — culture sets the intention, but someone still has to make it physically impossible to pull the same metric five different ways. How do you get three teams to agree on which version of truth is the real one when they each have evidence theirs is correct?

posts.post_text: Enterprise analytics teams are wasting 40% of their time on ad-hoc reporting requests. Our new AI-Powered Analytics eliminates the bottleneck entirely. See how Fortune 500 companies are scaling their data teams with ThoughtSpot. #analytics #enterprise
posts.angle: ThoughtSpot pushing 'eliminate the bottleneck entirely' enterprise framing — challenge the root cause assumption with mid-market reality
posts.draft_comment: Interesting framing — but I'd push back a little on the diagnosis. The 40% isn't really a bottleneck problem, it's a trust problem. Business teams keep submitting requests because they don't trust the numbers they'd get if they ran the query themselves. Faster delivery doesn't fix that.

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption problem (nobody knows what to ask) — validate the shadow AI insight and reframe the root cause as a data literacy gap, not a tooling gap
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is pretty common but the shadow AI detail is the more honest signal — people don't stop being curious, they just route around friction. The 'nobody knows what to ask' problem is usually a symptom though. It's less about training and more that the tool puts all the interpretive work back on the user. Did you find the 12% who did stick with it had something in common?
